name: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess

clinicalPearls: Overt single-nutrient deficiencies are uncommon in Western settings, but subclinical 'hidden hunger' is frequent in the elderly and the socioeconomically deprived; multiple deficiencies cluster in the chronically ill, those with alcohol use disorder, the impoverished, and post-bariatric-surgery patients.

Body stores differ enormously: vitamin B12 and vitamin A reserves are large (deficiency may take a year or more to appear), whereas folate and thiamine can be depleted within weeks of an inadequate diet.

Thiamine should be replenished before or during refeeding of malnourished or alcoholic patients, because giving carbohydrate (especially IV glucose) without thiamine can precipitate acute deficiency with lactic acidosis and Wernicke encephalopathy.

Wernicke encephalopathy is the classic triad of ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, cerebellar ataxia, and confusion; addition of memory loss and confabulation defines Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is underdiagnosed despite a typical history.

Pellagra (niacin deficiency) is remembered as the 'four Ds' - dermatitis (notably the photosensitive Casal's necklace), diarrhea, dementia, and death; it arises with corn-based diets, alcoholism, Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome, and isoniazid use.

Pyridoxine (B6) should be co-administered with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy; paradoxically, chronic high-dose B6 (above ~100 mg/d) itself causes a reversible severe sensory neuropathy, so long-term supplementation should be discouraged.

Vitamin A deficiency is the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide (xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia) and impairs immune defenses, increasing mortality from diarrhea, measles, malaria, and respiratory infection.

Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies (A, D, E, K) characteristically accompany fat-malabsorptive states such as celiac disease, cholestatic liver disease, cystic fibrosis, short-bowel syndrome, and bariatric surgery.

Zinc deficiency presents with growth retardation/dwarfism, hypogonadism, hypogeusia, alopecia, immune dysfunction, and a periorificial/acral rash; the inherited form is acrodermatitis enteropathica, and penicillamine or chronic zinc itself (via copper depletion) can be culprits.

Copper deficiency causes an anemia refractory to iron plus neutropenia and can be precipitated by chronic high-dose zinc; inherited disorders include Menkes kinky-hair syndrome (ATP7A) and aceruloplasminemia.

Selenium deficiency causes Keshan cardiomyopathy in low-soil regions; combined iodine and selenium deficiency can aggravate cretinism, while selenium excess causes selenosis (hair/nail loss, garlic breath, neuropathy).

Biotin and choline deficiencies occur mainly with inborn errors or parenteral nutrition; high-dose biotin supplements can spuriously skew streptavidin-biotin immunoassays (e.g., falsely high free T4, falsely low TSH or troponin).
harrison.pathophysiology: Vitamins are organic micronutrients that the body cannot synthesize in adequate amounts and that act largely as coenzymes or prosthetic groups (e.g., thiamine pyrophosphate in alpha-ketoacid decarboxylation; FAD/FMN flavoenzymes; NAD/NADP in redox reactions; pyridoxal phosphate in amino-acid metabolism). Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) require intact fat absorption and act in vision, gene transcription, calcium homeostasis, antioxidant defense, and gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors. Trace minerals function within metalloenzymes (zinc in numerous metalloenzymes and transcription factors; copper in ceruloplasmin/ferroxidase, cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase; selenium in glutathione peroxidase and deiodinases). Deficiency arises from inadequate intake, malabsorption, increased losses (hemodialysis, diuretics, increased urinary excretion), drug interference (isoniazid-B6, warfarin-vitamin K, metformin-B12/thiamine, penicillamine-zinc), or genetic transport/enzyme defects. Conversely, supplements, fortification, and occupational exposures can cause clinically important toxicities; in the inflammatory/acute-phase state, micronutrients redistribute and standard laboratory levels become unreliable.
additionalDifferentials: Malabsorption syndromes (celiac disease, Crohn's disease, short-bowel syndrome)
Inborn errors of metabolism affecting micronutrient handling (Hartnup disease, biotinidase deficiency, abetalipoproteinemia, Menkes/Wilson disease)
nonInfectiousMimics: Peripheral neuropathy from diabetes or heavy-metal toxicity (mimics thiamine, B6, B12, or vitamin E deficiency)
Dermatitis/seborrhea of other cause (mimics niacin, riboflavin, biotin, or zinc deficiency)
Megaloblastic anemia from drugs or marrow disease (mimics folate/B12 deficiency)
Pseudotumor cerebri or hypercalcemia of other etiology (mimics chronic vitamin A or D toxicity)
Coagulopathy of hepatic disease (mimics vitamin K deficiency - distinguished by failure of prothrombin time to correct with vitamin K)
additionalInvestigations: Erythrocyte transketolase activity with thiamine pyrophosphate stimulation (>25% / activity coefficient >1.25 abnormal); serum/blood thiamine by HPLC
Erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity for riboflavin; urinary 2-pyridone/2-methylnicotinamide for niacin
Plasma pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (deficiency <20 nmol/L) for vitamin B6; plasma/leukocyte ascorbate for vitamin C
Serum retinol (normal 1.05-3.50 micromol/L; deficient <0.70 micromol/L [20 microg/dL]) interpreted alongside C-reactive protein and alpha1-acid glycoprotein
Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (>20 ng/mL adequate for bone health); plasma alpha-tocopherol (deficient <5 microg/mL) for vitamin E
Prothrombin time and PIVKA-II (undercarboxylated prothrombin) plus serum phylloquinone (<0.15 microg/L) for vitamin K
Serum zinc (<12 micromol/L / <70 microg/dL), serum copper (<65 microg/dL) with ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL), interpreted with albumin and acute-phase status
redFlags: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, or ataxia in an alcoholic or malnourished patient before/during refeeding - possible Wernicke encephalopathy requiring immediate thiamine
High-output cardiac failure with edema (wet beriberi) or Keshan-type cardiomyopathy (selenium)
Night blindness, corneal xerosis, or keratomalacia signaling sight-threatening vitamin A deficiency
Bleeding/hemorrhage with prolonged prothrombin time, especially neonatal intracranial or GI bleeding (vitamin K deficiency)
Increased intracranial pressure, bulging fontanels, hypercalcemia, or papilledema suggesting vitamin A or D intoxication
Iron-refractory anemia with neutropenia (copper deficiency, often from chronic high-dose zinc)
harrison.prognosis: Most deficiency syndromes respond well and reversibly to timely repletion: thiamine produces cardiovascular and ophthalmoplegic improvement within ~24 hours and scurvy improves within days, although Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis may be permanent and vitamin E or B12 neurologic deficits may only partially recover if advanced. Vitamin A deficiency carries substantial mortality - keratomalacia blinds an estimated quarter-million children yearly with case-fatality of 4-25%, and supplementation in deficient populations reduces childhood mortality by roughly 23-34%. Untreated severe thiamine, niacin (death is the fourth 'D'), or selenium (Keshan) deficiency can be fatal, as can acute vitamin A or D intoxication.
pitfalls: Interpreting micronutrient blood levels during inflammation/acute illness without accounting for acute-phase redistribution (e.g., copper rises with ceruloplasmin, zinc and retinol fall), leading to over- or under-diagnosis
Refeeding a malnourished or alcoholic patient with carbohydrate before giving thiamine, precipitating acute deficiency and lactic acidosis
Attributing a prolonged prothrombin time solely to vitamin K deficiency in liver disease - if it fails to correct with vitamin K, the cause is hepatocellular
Overlooking drug-induced deficiencies (isoniazid-B6, warfarin/orlistat-vitamin K, metformin-B12, chronic zinc-copper, penicillamine-zinc) and chronic high-dose B6 causing neuropathy
Missing biotin supplement interference with streptavidin-biotin immunoassays (spurious thyroid, troponin, or hCG results)
Assuming carotenemia (yellow palms/soles, spared sclerae) indicates jaundice; and giving high-dose beta-carotene to smokers, which raises lung cancer risk
harrison.severityClassification: Deficiency severity is graded from subclinical/biochemical (laboratory abnormality without symptoms - 'hidden hunger') through overt clinical deficiency syndromes (beriberi, pellagra, scurvy, xerophthalmia, rickets) to life-threatening complications (Wernicke-Korsakoff, keratomalacia/blindness, hemorrhage, cardiomyopathy). Thiamine deficiency is classically dichotomized into wet (cardiovascular) and dry (neuropathic) beriberi with considerable overlap, and vitamin A xerophthalmia is staged from night blindness and conjunctival xerosis/Bitot's spots to corneal ulceration and keratomalacia.
management: Targeted repletion of the specific deficient vitamin or trace mineral by the oral or parenteral route according to severity and absorptive capacity
Parenteral thiamine given before or with any carbohydrate or intravenous glucose in malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy and lactic acidosis
Treat the underlying cause such as malabsorption, alcohol use disorder, restrictive diet or previous bariatric surgery, and address clustered multiple deficiencies together
Co-administer pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy, while avoiding chronic high-dose pyridoxine which itself causes a sensory neuropathy
Avoid over-supplementation and monitor for toxicity, particularly with the fat-soluble vitamins A and D
Monitor biochemical nutrient markers and watch for refeeding electrolyte shifts during nutritional rehabilitation
Involve a dietitian and nutrition support team for assessment, repletion planning and long-term dietary counselling
